## Quick Reference Card

### Key Questions to Ask

1. **What is the [level of measurement](#levels-of-measurement) of my [outcome variable](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557882/)?**
   - **Interval or ratio** (measured on a scale) → T-tests or Wilcoxon tests
   - **Ordinal with many levels** (e.g., pain 0–10) → Wilcoxon tests
   - **Nominal, or ordinal with few categories** (groups) → Chi-squared, Fisher's, or McNemar's

2. **Are my observations independent or paired?**
   - Independent: Different subjects in each group
   - Paired: Same subjects measured twice, or matched pairs

3. **For interval or ratio outcomes: Is the data normally distributed?**
   - Check with [histogram, Q-Q plot, or box plot](https://statisticsbyjim.com/basics/assessing-normality-histograms-probability-plots/)
   - If n > 30, [t-tests]{.test-2sample-t} are generally robust to non-normality

4. **For nominal or ordinal outcomes: Do any cells have fewer than 5 observations?**
   - Look at the smallest count in your [contingency table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contingency_table)
   - If any cell < 5, use [Fisher's exact test]{.test-fisher}

### Common Mistakes to Avoid

- Using [Chi-squared]{.test-chisq} when any cell has fewer than 5 observations
- Using [t-tests]{.test-2sample-t} on highly skewed data with small samples
- Treating paired data as independent (or vice versa)
- Using [McNemar's test]{.test-mcnemar} on unpaired nominal/ordinal data
- Treating an ordinal outcome (a single Likert item, a stage, a risk category) as if it were interval or ratio — averaging it without asking whether the spacing between values is really equal

## Levels of Measurement

Before you can pick a test, you have to name what *kind* of variable your outcome is. The standard vocabulary — the one used in your statistics coursework, by your DNP committee, and in most nursing journals — is the four **levels of measurement**: **nominal**, **ordinal**, **interval**, and **ratio**. The level tells you what your numbers actually *mean*, and therefore what arithmetic is honest to do with them.

Each level adds one property to the level before it:

| Level | Categories are... | Ordered? | Equal spacing between values? | True zero (zero means "none")? |
|:------|:------------------|:---------|:------------------------------|:-------------------------------|
| **Nominal** | Named labels only | No | No | No |
| **Ordinal** | Ranked labels | Yes | No | No |
| **Interval** | Numbers | Yes | Yes | No |
| **Ratio** | Numbers | Yes | Yes | Yes |

: The four levels of measurement {#tbl-levels}

### Nominal

Unordered labels. The categories differ in *kind*, not in *amount*. There is no meaningful way to rank them, so averages are meaningless — only counts and percentages.

**DNP examples:** unit assignment (ICU / med-surg / ED), central line infection (yes / no), insurance type (Medicare / Medicaid / commercial / self-pay), discharge disposition (home / SNF / rehab / expired), nurse licensure (RN / LPN).

> A quick check: if you shuffled the order of the categories on a chart and nothing was lost, the variable is nominal.

### Ordinal

Ordered categories, but the distance between adjacent categories is unknown and probably unequal. You can say *more* or *less*, but not *how much more*. Medians and ranks are appropriate; means are shaky.

**DNP examples:** pain rating 0–10, Likert satisfaction (strongly disagree → strongly agree), pressure injury stage (I / II / III / IV), Braden risk category (severe / high / moderate / mild), NYHA heart failure class (I–IV), triage acuity (ESI 1–5).

> The gap between pressure injury stage I and II is not the same clinical distance as the gap between stage III and IV — even though the labels are one number apart. That is what makes it ordinal rather than interval.

### Interval

Equal, meaningful distances between values, but the zero point is arbitrary rather than an absence of the thing. Differences are interpretable; ratios are not.

**DNP examples:** temperature in °F or °C, calendar year, standardized test scores with an arbitrary origin.

> 40 °C is not "twice as hot" as 20 °C, because 0 °C does not mean "no temperature." Differences still work fine: a 2-degree rise is a 2-degree rise anywhere on the scale.

### Ratio

Everything interval has, plus a true zero meaning "none of it." Differences *and* ratios are both interpretable — this is the most informative level.

**DNP examples:** length of stay in days, weight in kg, systolic blood pressure in mmHg, hemoglobin A1c, minutes to first ambulation, falls per 1,000 patient-days, number of readmissions.

> A 10-day stay really is twice as long as a 5-day stay, because 0 days means no stay at all.

### From Level of Measurement to Test

For the seven tests in this guide, **interval and ratio behave identically** — that distinction matters for how you *describe* your results, not for which test you run. What actually drives test selection is whether your outcome can be meaningfully averaged or ranked, versus counted up in a table:

- **Interval or ratio** → compare **means** with a [t-test]{.test-2sample-t}, or **ranks** with a [Wilcoxon]{.test-wilcox-rank} test if the data are skewed.
- **Ordinal with many ordered levels** (e.g., pain 0–10, a summed Likert scale) → compare **ranks** with a [Wilcoxon]{.test-wilcox-rank} test.
- **Nominal, or ordinal with only a few categories** → **count** people in a contingency table and use [Chi-Squared]{.test-chisq}, [Fisher's Exact]{.test-fisher}, or [McNemar's]{.test-mcnemar}.

The [Decision Matrix](#decision-matrix) below carries this all the way to a specific test, once you add whether your groups are independent or paired.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Ordinal is the one that trips people up

Ordinal is the only level that can go either way, and where it lands depends on how many levels it has.

- **Few ordered categories** (e.g., "improved / unchanged / worsened") → count them in a contingency table and use [Chi-Squared]{.test-chisq}, [Fisher's Exact]{.test-fisher}, or [McNemar's]{.test-mcnemar}.
- **Many ordered levels** (e.g., a 0–10 pain scale, a summed Likert scale) → the [Wilcoxon]{.test-wilcox-rank} tests are the safe default. They work on **ranks**, which is exactly what ordinal data supports, so they do not require you to pretend the spacing between values is equal.

Running a t-test on an ordinal outcome is a very common shortcut. It is defensible for a long, well-behaved scale with a large sample, but the rank-based Wilcoxon test is the more honest choice — and with the same data it usually reaches the same conclusion, so there is little to lose by using it.
:::

**Color Key:** Tests are color-coded by family (colorblind-friendly palette)

- **Blue shades**: T-tests (parametric; interval or ratio outcomes)
- **Orange shades**: Wilcoxon tests (non-parametric; interval, ratio, or many-level ordinal outcomes)
- **Green shades**: Contingency table tests (nominal outcomes, or ordinal with few categories)
:::

|:---------------------|:-------|:------------------|:-----------------|
| Interval / Ratio | Independent | Normal | [**2-Sample T-Test**](#sample-t-test-independent-samples){.test-2sample-t} ([Helpful video](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/ap-statistics/xfb5d8e68:inference-quantitative-means/two-sample-t-test-means/v/two-sample-t-test-for-difference-of-means)) |
| Interval / Ratio, or Ordinal (many levels) | Independent | Non-normal/Skewed | [**Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test**](#wilcoxon-rank-sum-test-mann-whitney-u){.test-wilcox-rank} ([Helpful video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AM87jjnNt8U)) |
| Interval / Ratio | Paired/Matched | Normal | [**Paired T-Test**](#paired-t-test){.test-paired-t} ([Helpful video](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/ap-statistics/xfb5d8e68:inference-quantitative-means/two-sample-t-test-means/v/example-of-hypotheses-for-paired-and-2-sample-t-tests)) |
| Interval / Ratio, or Ordinal (many levels) | Paired/Matched | Non-normal/Skewed | [**Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test**](#wilcoxon-signed-rank-test){.test-wilcox-signed} ([Helpful video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4XdhxQ3THS0)) |
| Nominal, or Ordinal (few categories) | Independent | Large sample (all cells ≥ 5) | [**Chi-Squared Test**](#chi-squared-test){.test-chisq} ([Helpful video](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/ap-statistics/chi-square-tests/chi-square-goodness-fit/v/chi-square-statistic)) |
| Nominal, or Ordinal (few categories) | Independent | Small sample (any cell < 5) | [**Fisher's Exact Test**](#fishers-exact-test){.test-fisher} ([Helpful video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W_wqly6Fr-o)) |
| Nominal, or Ordinal (few categories) | Paired/Matched | Any | [**McNemar's Test**](#mcnemars-test){.test-mcnemar} ([Helpful video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lbkdvDTXVQM)) |

## Key Terms Explained

**Level of Measurement** (see [Levels of Measurement](#levels-of-measurement) for the full definitions and examples)**:**

- **Nominal:** Unordered labels (e.g., yes/no, pass/fail, infected/not infected, unit assignment).
- **Ordinal:** Ordered categories with unequal spacing (e.g., pain 0–10, Likert satisfaction, pressure injury stage).
- **Interval:** Equal spacing, but no true zero (e.g., temperature in °F).
- **Ratio:** Equal spacing and a true zero (e.g., length of stay in days, weight in kg, mmHg).

**Groups:**

- **Independent:** Different people in each group. Example: 50 patients get Treatment A, a *different* 50 patients get Treatment B.
- **Paired/Matched:** Same people measured twice, or intentionally matched pairs. Example: Measuring the *same* 50 patients before AND after an intervention.

**Distribution (for interval, ratio, or many-level ordinal outcomes):**

- **Normal:** Data is roughly symmetric and bell-shaped. Most values cluster around the middle, with fewer extreme values. Common with large samples (n > 30).
- **Non-normal/Skewed:** Data is lopsided—bunched up on one end with a long tail. Common with small samples, scores with floor/ceiling effects, or counts.

**Cell counts (for nominal or few-category ordinal outcomes):**

When your outcome is nominal (or ordinal with just a few categories), you create a contingency table counting how many people fall into each combination:

|                    | Outcome Yes | Outcome No |
|--------------------|-------------|------------|
| **Intervention**   | 8           | 42         |
| **Control**        | 22          | 38         |

- **All cells ≥ 5:** Every box in the table has 5 or more people → use Chi-Squared
- **Any cell < 5:** At least one box has fewer than 5 people → use Fisher's Exact

:::

## Test Descriptions

### Tests for Interval, Ratio, or Many-Level Ordinal Outcomes

#### [2-Sample T-Test]{.test-2sample-t} (Independent Samples)

**Use when:**

- Comparing means between two independent groups
- Outcome variable is interval or ratio
- Data is approximately normally distributed (or n > 30 per group)

**Null hypothesis:** The population means of the two groups are equal.

**Scenario:** Comparing systolic blood pressure (mmHg) between patients who received enhanced discharge education vs. standard care.

| Patient | Group | Systolic BP (mmHg) |
|---------|-------|--------------------|
| 1       | Enhanced | 120 |
| 2       | Enhanced | 135 |
| 3       | Enhanced | 142 |
| 4       | Standard | 110 |
| 5       | Standard | 118 |
| 6       | Standard | 125 |

---

#### [Paired T-Test]{.test-paired-t}

**Use when:**

- Comparing means between two related measurements
- Same subjects measured twice (before/after)
- Differences are approximately normally distributed

**Null hypothesis:** The mean difference between paired observations is zero.

**Scenario:** Measuring systolic blood pressure (mmHg) in the same patients before and 3 months after implementing a hypertension self-management program.

| Patient | Pre (mmHg) | Post (mmHg) | Change |
|---------|------------|-------------|--------|
| 1       | 152        | 138         | -14    |
| 2       | 168        | 155         | -13    |
| 3       | 145        | 140         | -5     |
| 4       | 159        | 148         | -11    |
| 5       | 171        | 158         | -13    |

---

#### [Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test]{.test-wilcox-rank} (Mann-Whitney U)

**Use when:**

- Comparing two independent groups
- Outcome is interval, ratio, or ordinal
- Data is not normally distributed or sample size is small

**Null hypothesis:** The distributions of the two groups are equal.

**Scenario:** Comparing patient satisfaction scores (1-10 scale) between units using bedside shift report vs. traditional nurse station handoff.

| Patient | Handoff Type | Satisfaction (1-10) |
|---------|--------------|---------------------|
| 1       | Bedside     | 8 |
| 2       | Bedside     | 9 |
| 3       | Bedside     | 7 |
| 4       | Traditional | 5 |
| 5       | Traditional | 6 |
| 6       | Traditional | 7 |

---

#### [Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test]{.test-wilcox-signed}

**Use when:**

- Comparing two related measurements (same subjects measured twice)
- Data is not normally distributed
- Ordinal data or skewed differences

**Null hypothesis:** The median difference between pairs is zero.

**Scenario:** Measuring post-operative pain (0-10 NRS) in the same patients before and after implementing a guided imagery intervention.

| Patient | Pre (0-10) | Post (0-10) | Change |
|---------|------------|-------------|--------|
| 1       | 7          | 4           | -3     |
| 2       | 8          | 5           | -3     |
| 3       | 6          | 4           | -2     |
| 4       | 9          | 6           | -3     |
| 5       | 8          | 5           | -3     |

---

### Tests for Nominal or Few-Category Ordinal Outcomes

#### [Chi-Squared Test]{.test-chisq}

**Use when:**

- Testing association between two nominal (or few-category ordinal) variables
- All cells have 5 or more observations
- Independent observations (different people in each cell)

**Null hypothesis:** The two variables are independent.

**Scenario:** Comparing rates of hospital-acquired pressure injuries (HAPI) between units that implemented a new skin assessment bundle vs. units using standard care.

|                    | HAPI Yes | HAPI No | Row Total |
|--------------------|----------|---------|-----------|
| **New Bundle**     | 12       | 88      | 100       |
| **Standard Care**  | 28       | 72      | 100       |
| **Column Total**   | 40       | 160     | 200       |

---

#### [Fisher's Exact Test]{.test-fisher}

**Use when:**

- Testing association between two nominal (or few-category ordinal) variables
- Any cell has fewer than 5 observations
- Small sample sizes

**Null hypothesis:** The two variables are independent.

**Scenario:** Pilot study comparing CLABSI rates between ICU patients receiving a new central line maintenance bundle vs. standard protocol (small sample).

|                  | CLABSI | No CLABSI | Row Total |
|------------------|--------|-----------|-----------|
| **New Bundle**   | 1      | 11        | 12        |
| **Standard**     | 6      | 6         | 12        |
| **Column Total** | 7      | 17        | 24        |

**Rule of thumb:** If your smallest cell has fewer than 5 observations (here: 1), use Fisher's Exact Test instead of Chi-Squared.

---

#### [McNemar's Test]{.test-mcnemar}

**Use when:**

- Paired nominal data (2×2 table)
- **Same subjects** measured at two time points
- Testing whether change occurred in one direction more than the other

**Null hypothesis:** The probability of changing from A to B equals the probability of changing from B to A.

**Scenario:** Testing whether nurses' hand hygiene compliance changed after a QI intervention, with the same 100 nurses observed before and after.

|                         | **After: Compliant** | **After: Non-compliant** | Row Total |
|-------------------------|----------------------|--------------------------|-----------|
| **Before: Compliant**   | 45 (stayed compliant)| 15 (became non-compliant)| 60        |
| **Before: Non-compliant**| 25 (became compliant)| 15 (stayed non-compliant)| 40        |
| **Column Total**        | 70                   | 30                       | 100       |

**Key Difference from [Chi-Squared]{.test-chisq}:**

- **[Chi-Squared]{.test-chisq}/[Fisher's]{.test-fisher}:** 100 different people
- **[McNemar's]{.test-mcnemar}:** Same 100 nurses observed twice
- **Focus cells:** Only the **off-diagonal** cells matter (15 got worse vs. 25 improved)

---

## Interpreting for Practice

When reporting statistical results for your DNP project, use the **3 S's** mnemonic to ensure you communicate findings clearly and meaningfully:

::: {.callout-important}
## The 3 S's: Sign, Size, Significance

1. **[Sign]{.interpret-sign}** — What is the *direction* of the effect? (increase/decrease, higher/lower, more/less)
2. **[Size]{.interpret-size}** — What is the *magnitude* of the effect? (How much did it change? Is it clinically meaningful?)
3. **[Significance]{.interpret-significance}** — What does the *p-value* tell us? ([Do we have sufficient evidence to rule out sampling variability?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EYX-QDNvlt4))
:::

Always report results in this order. The effect size (magnitude) is often more important for practice decisions than the p-value alone.

---

### Example 1: Paired T-Test for Blood Pressure

**Result (APA 7):** A paired-samples *t*-test indicated that systolic blood pressure was lower after the self-management program (*M* = 148 mmHg, *SE* = 3.2) than before (*M* = 159 mmHg, *SE* = 4.1), *t*(24) = 3.44, *p* = .002, 95% CI [4.2, 17.8].

**Interpretation:**

"Following the self-management program, patients' systolic blood pressure [decreased]{.interpret-sign} by an average of 11 mmHg. [This reduction is clinically meaningful because a 10 mmHg decrease in systolic BP is associated with approximately 20% reduced risk of major cardiovascular events.]{.interpret-size} [Given p = .002 and the 95% CI [4.2, 17.8] excludes zero, there is sufficient evidence to rule out sampling variability.]{.interpret-significance}"

**Why this works:**
- [**Sign:**]{.interpret-sign} "decreased" clearly indicates direction
- [**Size:**]{.interpret-size} Quantifies the change (11 mmHg) AND argues for clinical meaningfulness
- [**Significance:**]{.interpret-significance} Uses p-value and CI to address whether we can rule out chance

---

### Example 2: Chi-Squared Test for Pressure Injuries

**Result (APA 7):** A chi-square test of independence showed an association between the skin assessment bundle and HAPI occurrence, χ²(1, *N* = 200) = 8.2, *p* = .004. HAPI rates were 12% with the new bundle versus 28% with standard care.

**Interpretation:**

"Hospital-acquired pressure injury rates were [lower]{.interpret-sign} in units using the new bundle (12%) compared to standard care (28%)—a 16 percentage point absolute reduction. [This reduction is clinically meaningful because each HAPI is associated with extended hospital stays, increased costs (~$10,000–$25,000 per event), and significant patient suffering.]{.interpret-size} [Given χ²(1) = 8.2, p = .004, there is sufficient evidence to rule out sampling variability.]{.interpret-significance}"

**Why this works:**
- [**Sign:**]{.interpret-sign} "lower" indicates the favorable direction
- [**Size:**]{.interpret-size} Both percentages (12% vs 28%) quantify magnitude AND the argument connects to patient outcomes and costs
- [**Significance:**]{.interpret-significance} Uses p-value to address whether we can rule out chance

---

### Example 3: Results Without Sufficient Evidence

**Result (APA 7):** A Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated that pain scores after guided imagery (Mdn = 6) were not statistically different from pain scores before (Mdn = 7), *Z* = -1.55, *p* = .121.

**Interpretation:**

"Pain scores [decreased]{.interpret-sign} by a median of 1 point on the 0-10 NRS following guided imagery. [A 1-point reduction, while potentially noticeable to patients, falls below the 2-point threshold often considered the minimal clinically important difference for acute pain.]{.interpret-size} [However, with p = .121, there was insufficient evidence to rule out sampling variability.]{.interpret-significance}"

**Why this works:**
- [**Sign:**]{.interpret-sign} Still report the direction observed
- [**Size:**]{.interpret-size} Reports the magnitude (1 point) AND discusses whether it meets clinical thresholds
- [**Significance:**]{.interpret-significance} Honest about evidence limitations—p-value suggests we cannot rule out chance

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key Takeaway

Never report p-values alone. Always include:
- The direction of change
- The magnitude with appropriate units and confidence intervals
- A statement about clinical or practical meaningfulness

**Marcus pet peeve:** Avoid saying results are "statistically significant" or "not significant." Instead, focus on what the data tell us about clinical importance.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Using AI to Learn Statistical Tests (Without Compromising PHI)

AI tools like Microsoft Copilot can help you learn how to run statistical tests—but **never enter real patient data**. Instead, ask the AI to generate a toy example with made-up data.

**Example prompt:**

> "I need to conduct a pairwise t-test in Microsoft Excel, but I need an example to follow, including how I structure my data. Give me a toy example so I can learn using made up data from 18 individuals taking the PHQ-9 before therapy and after 6 months of cognitive behavioral therapy."

[See Copilot's response to this prompt](https://copilot.microsoft.com/shares/pttziuLuusCiaGmhhxdKT)

This approach is:

- **Safe** — No PHI is shared with AI tools
- **Reproducible** — You follow each step manually and document what you did, creating an audit trail that a statistician or mentor can verify
- **Educational** — You learn by working through a realistic example

The AI is an *instructional resource*, not the analyst—you remain the analyst. This avoids the "black box" problem where data goes into an AI and results come out with no way to verify what happened in between.
:::
